metadata.title: PIRLS 2001 Technical Report
metadata.venue: International Association for the Evaluation of Educational Achievement (IEA) International Study Center

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The PIRLS 2001 technical report documents a two-stage probability-proportional-to-size sampling design: first, at least 150 schools per country were selected using probability-proportional-to-size sampling (with optional stratification variables such as urbanicity or school type), and second, one or two fourth-grade classes were randomly sampled within each selected school. The report states that sampling weights were computed by Statistics Canada and that countries were weighted so that each participating country contributed equally to the international mean and standard deviation of the achievement scale (scale average set to 500, SD to 100). The excerpt provided does not specify the exact student weight variable name(s) or whether replicate weights (e.g., BRR/jackknife) were used for variance estimation, so those details cannot be extracted here. For analysts using the PIRLS international database, the intended practice is to apply the provided PIRLS sampling weights for student-level estimates and to follow the report’s scaling/conditioning procedures when producing comparable achievement statistics across countries.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an official IEA/OECD technical report or assessment framework. It describes sampling, scaling, and instrument design rather than student-level predictive modeling. Plausible values are therefore not applicable to the document's primary analytic purpose; any missing-data discussion refers to fieldwork or scaling procedures, not a single ML imputation strategy.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report describes the target population as fourth-grade students (the upper of the two grades with the most 9-year-olds) assessed near the end of the school year in each participating country. Within each country, representative samples were selected using a two-stage design: probability-proportional-to-size selection of at least 150 schools, followed by random sampling of one or two fourth-grade classes per school. The excerpt does not specify additional analytic exclusions (e.g., missing questionnaire items, incomplete booklet completion, or specific item-level filters), so the intended analytic sample is the full available student sample generated by this sampling design, with achievement scaling based on the matrix-sampled test booklets.

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2001 is a cross-national reading literacy assessment of fourth-grade students (upper of the two grades with the most 9-year-olds) administered near the end of the school year in 35 participating countries. The assessment uses a matrix sampling design: reading passages are organized into eight 40-minute blocks (four literary and four informational) distributed across 10 test booklets, with each student completing one booklet in an 80-minute session. Achievement is scaled primarily using item response theory (2-parameter, 3-parameter, and generalized partial credit models) and is reported on a common scale (international mean 500, SD 100), with conditioning on background questionnaires and multiple imputation to generate plausible values for analysis and reporting. The report also describes four international achievement benchmarks (25th, 50th, 75th, 90th percentiles) and scale anchoring to interpret what students can do at each benchmark. Sampling is two-stage (schools then classes), and the report emphasizes rigorous translation verification, data cleaning, and quality control for constructed-response scoring across countries.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a PIRLS 2001 technical report describing assessment design, sampling, instrument development, translation verification, data processing, scaling, and reporting procedures rather than an empirical machine-learning study with predictive targets. As such, it does not provide student-level ML model training/evaluation results, distinct dependent variables for ML prediction, or algorithm comparisons; therefore main_findings and confounders_identified are intentionally empty. The report does, however, specify the intended achievement scaling approach (IRT with conditioning and multiple imputation to plausible values) and the sampling framework needed to interpret PIRLS achievement estimates.
